title: Case 1: The Blackwood File
story_template: {opening}. Before the senior detectives hand you the full registry, they want you to pull a small sample of suspects tied to the case file.
description: Show the first 5 suspects from the suspects table.
hints: This case is only about reading data, not filtering it.
Use SELECT * to return every column, then keep the result small with LIMIT.
LIMIT controls how many rows SQLite returns. You need only 5 rows.
success_explanation: You inspected a manageable slice of the registry by returning all columns but limiting the result to five rows.
case_update_template: The first five records give the academy a starting pool of names, ages, cities, and occupations. One pattern stands out immediately: Riverton appears more than once, and the detectives decide that city deserves the next look in the {case_name} investigation.

title: Case 2: The Riverton Lead
story_template: Witnesses say someone connected to {victim} fled toward Riverton before dawn after the trouble at {scene}. The lead detective wants a clean briefing sheet that lists only the people in the suspect registry tied to that city.
description: Find the names and cities of all suspects located in Riverton.
expected_query: SELECT name, city FROM suspects WHERE city = 'Riverton';
hints: The answer should return only two columns: name and city.
Use WHERE to keep only rows where the city matches Riverton.
A WHERE clause filters rows. Keep the selected columns narrow so the result matches the briefing request.
success_explanation: You filtered the registry to one city and returned only the fields the briefing asked for.
case_update_template: The Riverton list is shorter than the full registry, which sharpens the case. A follow-up sweep around {scene} suggests the killer or an accomplice may have returned to a secured location after {victim}'s death.

title: Case 3: Midnight Entry
story_template: Investigators recovered access logs from a nearby secure site linked to {scene}. To rebuild the timeline after {victim}'s death, the academy wants the single most recent entry from that log.
description: Show the suspect_id, location_id, access_date, and access_time for the most recent access log entry.
expected_query: SELECT suspect_id, location_id, access_date, access_time FROM access_logs ORDER BY access_date DESC, access_time DESC LIMIT 1;
hints: Return exactly four columns: suspect_id, location_id, access_date, and access_time.
Use ORDER BY to sort from newest to oldest, then keep one row with LIMIT.
DESC means descending order, so larger or later values appear first. That helps you bring the newest date and time to the top.
success_explanation: You ranked the logs by recency and isolated the newest entry for the investigation timeline.
case_update_template: The newest access record places a suspect near a protected site after the crime window. That pushes the academy toward a financial motive tied to {motive}, so the next step is to find who has the heaviest transaction activity.

title: Case 4: Money Trail
story_template: A forensic accountant finds a cluster of suspicious transfers around the night of the crime at {scene}. Before anyone starts naming names, the academy wants a simple summary that shows which suspect_id appears most often in the bank transactions table.
description: Show the suspect_id and transaction count for the suspect with the highest number of bank transactions.
expected_query: SELECT suspect_id, COUNT(*) AS transaction_count FROM bank_transactions GROUP BY suspect_id ORDER BY transaction_count DESC LIMIT 1;
hints: The result should have two columns: suspect_id and a transaction count.
Count how many transaction rows belong to each suspect_id, then rank those counts.
GROUP BY builds one group per suspect_id. DESC sorts the largest count first so LIMIT 1 can keep the top result.
success_explanation: You grouped the transactions by suspect_id, counted the rows, and isolated the busiest financial trail.
case_update_template: One suspect rises above the others in the money trail around {stolen_item}, but the chief still needs something tangible before making an arrest. The academy now turns to the evidence room to connect a person directly to a physical clue.

title: Case 5: Final Link
story_template: The final board is almost ready. To close the {case_name}, the academy must connect each physical evidence item to the suspect attached to it and present the result in a briefing-friendly form.
description: Show the suspect name and evidence type for every suspect linked to an evidence item.
expected_query: SELECT s.name, e.evidence_type FROM suspects s JOIN evidence_inventory e ON s.suspect_id = e.linked_suspect_id;
hints: The result should contain two columns: the suspect name and the evidence type.
Use a JOIN because the name is in suspects and the evidence link is in evidence_inventory.
A JOIN connects rows from two tables through matching keys. Here, suspect_id is the link to look for.
success_explanation: You combined two related tables so the academy could see people and evidence together in one result.
case_update_template: The evidence wall finally locks the timeline, the money trail, and the physical clues into one coherent picture. The academy closes the {case_name}, names the culprit behind {victim}'s death, and your first investigation ends with the crime solved.
